name: Tag Question
pattern: Anchor:Clause[declarative | exclamative] + Tag:Clause[Head:VP[Head:V[auxiliary]]; Subject:NP[personal pronoun]; surface Auxiliary–Subject (+ not)] => Meaning:Question

entry.name: Tag Question
entry.pattern: Anchor:Clause[declarative | exclamative] + Tag:Clause[Head:VP[Head:V[auxiliary]]; Subject:NP[personal pronoun]; surface Auxiliary–Subject (+ not)] => Meaning:Question

dimensions.form: A declarative or exclamative Anchor Clause followed by a supplementary short closed-interrogative Tag Clause; the tag has a personal-pronoun Subject and an auxiliary-headed VP, with surface subject–auxiliary inversion
dimensions.meaning: A normally biased polar question anchored to the proposition of the first Clause; polarity relation and prosody distinguish reversed- and constant-polarity interpretations
dimensions.function: Seeks verification, acknowledgement, agreement, or uptake of the anchor, with exclamative anchors normally supporting acknowledgement or rhetorical force rather than doubt
dimensions.distribution: Independent utterances in which a declarative or exclamative Clause licenses a following supplementary Tag Clause

1.specialization: A reversed-polarity tag presents a biased polar answer set whose salient positive member confirms the anchor proposition. A rising tag asks for verification or expresses doubt; a falling tag seeks acknowledgement and may be rhetorical. Exclamative anchors normally take this falling pattern because the truth of their proposition is presented as not at issue.

examples.note: Positive declarative Anchor Clause plus negative Tag Clause; reversed polarity
Tag auxiliary agrees with plural tag Subject they, not directly with singular anchor Subject everybody

examples.form: [What a mess I've made of things], [haven't I]?
examples.note: Exclamative Anchor Clause with the normally falling, acknowledgement-oriented reversed tag

2.specialization: A constant-polarity tag has the same polarity as its typically positive declarative anchor. With its characteristic slight rise, it commonly attributes the anchor content to the addressee and conveys acknowledgement, surprise, disapproval, reproach, or sarcasm rather than speaker doubt.

examples.note: Positive declarative anchor and positive tag; constant polarity

examples.form: [So you have forgotten your homework again], [have you]?
examples.note: Constant-polarity tag with reproachful or disapproving force

constraints.description: The construction combines an Anchor Clause with a supplementary Tag Clause; it does not turn their combination into a single Clause. Each Clause independently has the strict structure (Subject +) Head:VP.

The Anchor is a declarative or exclamative Clause. The Tag is a short closed-interrogative Clause with a personal-pronoun Subject and a VP headed by an auxiliary; subject–auxiliary inversion determines surface order.
If the relevant anchor Predicator is auxiliary-headed, the tag normally selects the same auxiliary lexeme; otherwise it selects do. The tag auxiliary normally has the anchor's tense.

The personal-pronoun tag Subject repeats a pronominal anchor Subject or is anaphorically selected for a non-pronominal one. Person–number agreement is controlled by the tag Subject, as Everybody has read it, haven't they? demonstrates.
A negative tag permits synthetic auxiliary negation in ordinary style or analytic final not in more formal style.

The tag has polarity opposite to the anchor in the frequent reversed-polarity variant and the same polarity in the constant-polarity variant; semantically negative anchors such as Few of them liked it select a positive reversed tag.

Prosody is constructionally significant: a reversed rising tag normally requests verification, a reversed falling tag seeks acknowledgement, and a constant tag characteristically has a slight rise with attributional or emotive effects.

projection.target: Recognizing Tag Question membership predicts an anaphoric personal-pronoun Subject, same-auxiliary selection or do-support, preservation of relevant tense, agreement with the tag Subject, a systematic reversed-or-constant polarity relation, and prosody-sensitive verification, acknowledgement, or emotive force
projection.evidence: The predictions jointly distinguish direct tags from arbitrary interrogative supplements: anchor Subject and Predicator determine pronoun, auxiliary, tense, and agreement, while polarity relation and contour predict the characteristic interpretations

grounds.note: Provides the direct tag-formation procedure and the polarity-by-prosody interpretation contrasts
The pronoun, auxiliary, tense, agreement, polarity, and prosody cluster recurs across declarative and exclamative anchors

known_boundary_items: CGEL also attests tags with closed-interrogative and imperative anchors; those lie outside this declarative-or-exclamative-anchor constructional node.
Lovely day, isn't it? has a non-clausal anchor under the strict VP-headed Clause ontology and therefore is not an instance of this Clause-anchored node.
Interrogative parentheticals such as don't you think? are larger interrogative supplements, not auxiliary-plus-pronoun tags.

relatedConstructions.notes: Tag Question inherits answer-set semantics and specializes it as an anchor-dependent, normally biased polar question
Both Anchor and Tag satisfy (Subject +) Head:VP; their supplemented combination is not itself a Clause

The short Tag is a closed-interrogative Clause with surface subject–auxiliary inversion

Non-clausal anchors in forms such as Lovely day, isn't it? require a separate host analysis

grounds.note: Describes anchor-plus-tag questions, direct tag formation, polarity classes, agreement, and prosodically conditioned interpretations

Tag Question is a semantic specialization realized by a declarative or exclamative Anchor Clause plus a Tag Clause with a pronominal Subject and auxiliary-headed VP; every Clause remains strictly VP-headed

curious.title: Questions tacked onto the end of a statement
curious.summary: A short question such as isn't he? can follow a statement to ask the listener to confirm it or react to it.
curious.body:
In He is ill, isn't he?, a short question follows the statement. It's built from an auxiliary verb and a pronoun that refers back to the person in the statement: isn't he. In the frequent version the question has the opposite polarity from the statement, positive then negative. A rising voice asks for confirmation, and a falling one invites agreement or acknowledgement.

A tag can also repeat the statement's polarity: He is ill, is he? This version can express surprise, disapproval or sarcasm, not doubt. The pronoun decides the verb's form, as in Everybody has read it, haven't they?

This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: [What a mess I've made of things], [haven't I]?
[So you have forgotten your homework again], [have you]?

curious.try: Say He is ill, isn't he? once with your voice rising at the end and once with it falling. Which version asks and which one invites agreement?

teacher.summary: Core material for tag questions: how the tag is formed and how polarity and intonation change its force.
teacher.explain: A tag question pairs an anchor clause (a declarative or exclamative) with a short closed-interrogative tag clause. The tag has a personal-pronoun subject and an auxiliary-headed VP, with subject-auxiliary inversion. If the anchor's predicator is headed by an auxiliary, the tag normally selects the same auxiliary; otherwise it uses do. The tag normally keeps the anchor's tense, and the verb agrees with the tag's pronoun. In the frequent reversed-polarity variant, a rising tag asks for verification and a falling tag seeks acknowledgement. A constant-polarity tag characteristically has a slight rise and can convey surprise, disapproval, reproach or sarcasm. Prosody is part of the construction. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional, though confidence in the pattern is marked high.
teacher.terms: Question tag is a textbook name. CGEL: tag clause attached to an anchor clause. The polarity relation is reversed or constant.

examples.text: [What a mess I've made of things], [haven't I]?
[So you have forgotten your homework again], [have you]?

contrasts.note: Reversed polarity; positive anchor, negative tag.
Constant polarity; slight rise, attributing the content to the addressee.

contrasts.text: Few of them liked it, did they?
contrasts.note: A semantically negative anchor takes a positive reversed tag.

watch_for: A learner might choose the tag verb to agree with a singular anchor subject such as everybody, when the tag's pronoun, they, controls agreement.
A learner might repeat the full verb from the anchor instead of using do when the anchor has no auxiliary.
A learner might ignore the intonation and miss whether the speaker wants confirmation or only agreement.
teacher.activity: Pairs say the same anchor, such as It's cold today, with different tags and intonation. The listener decides whether each version asks for confirmation, invites agreement or sounds surprised. Then they swap roles with new anchors.

child.hook: How do you ask a friend to agree with something you just said?
child.explain: A tag question is a tiny question stuck on the end of a sentence. It uses a short helper word like is, has or does, and a pronoun like he or she. Your voice rising or falling changes what you mean.
child.play: Say a sentence about a friend, then add a tiny question to check it. Say it twice, with your voice going up and then down. Does it sound different?

checked.note: Fixed: child.explain no longer says the tag repeats the helper word (the dictionary has the tag use do when the anchor's predicator has no auxiliary, as in She likes tea, doesn't she?); teacher.explain now ties auxiliary repetition to the anchor's predicator and says the constant-polarity rise is characteristic and its effects possible; replaced 'the entry' with 'this dictionary' and 'the usual textbook name' with 'a textbook name'.
